responses.response: Use a full validation pass because this is a pre-commit structural change. First, confirm the shared taxonomy through the shared spec files so the worker container kind, allowed relationship kinds, and any valid tags are correct. Second, inspect the main model file and make sure the new worker is under the correct parent system, its FQN is consistent everywhere, and any instanceOf target resolves if deployment files were touched. Third, validate relationships touching the worker: use only declared logical kinds such as calls, async, reads, writes, or uses; keep protocol or transport in technology; do not use deployment relationships to represent normal application traffic. Fourth, validate the dedicated C2 view: confirm the parent system boundary is visible, the worker appears with the intended neighboring containers and actors, and the include scope is narrow rather than something broad like include all. Fifth, check editor problems for unknown kinds, unresolved FQNs, bad nested references, or syntax issues. Sixth, preview the impacted C2 view and confirm there are no surprise elements, missing parents, or layout workarounds hiding a real reference problem. Seventh, if interactive validation is available later, follow up with project summary, relationship lookup, and view preview to verify kinds, edges, and rendering end to end.

Validate it as a focused C2 quick check. Parent context rule: a C2 view must show the parent system plus the containers and neighbors in scope. If the view only shows the user, web application, and API, confirm the enclosing system boundary is still visible; otherwise the view has lost required context. Inspect the include lines and prefer explicit elements or a tight system-scoped pattern. Treat a fully broad include as a red flag because it can pull in unrelated siblings and make the view look correct by accident. Confirm the view contains only the intended actor and container neighbors for this scenario, not extra systems or containers that happen to match a broad include. Check for unresolved FQNs, ambiguous references, or syntax issues in the editor problems. Then preview the view and ask two questions: do I still see the parent system boundary, and did any unexpected elements appear? If either answer is wrong, tighten the include list.

Treat this as more than a syntax check. First, re-check the semantics: async should mean one-way, non-blocking communication. If the interaction is actually request and response, calls was probably the correct model and the odd C2 view is warning you about a semantic mismatch. Second, confirm the relationship kind is valid in the shared taxonomy and that the edge still connects the correct container FQNs. Third, inspect the edge details: keep protocol or transport in technology, keep a meaningful label on the relationship, and do not invent a fake return path just to make the diagram look balanced. Fourth, validate the logical model itself: normal application traffic belongs in the logical model; do not duplicate the same app traffic as deployment-only relationships. Fifth, re-check the C2 view against parent-context rules: the parent system must still be visible, and the include scope must not be so broad or narrow that it distorts the async flow. Sixth, if the async interaction is really mediated by a queue or event bus, a direct container-to-container async edge may be syntactically valid but conceptually incomplete; the missing messaging element is often the real issue. Finish with problems and rendering review, and if syntax is clean but the behavior still feels wrong, trust that signal: the relationship may need to revert to calls or be remodeled through an explicit messaging container.
